messages.name: Toshihide Hige
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: training and feedback in an adult fly model
messages.body:
Dear Professor Hige,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. Chess and the public adult fly connectome led me to ask whether a model constrained by that wiring could learn useful decisions through experience and feedback.

Your lab's work linking mushroom-body synaptic plasticity to action selection is relevant to two connected questions: which identified reinforcement pathways should carry feedback, and how should training experiences be sequenced and spaced? I hope to begin with simple associations before introducing chess puzzles.

In all six simple tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the other option in only three tests. So it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound, and the chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser and hope to develop a scientifically sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Would you consider occasional mentorship, starting with whether the training schedule and reinforcement targets are defensible? I would appreciate a candid assessment of the approach and can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,
Ethan Ramli
High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

messages.name: Adam Claridge-Chang
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: reward delivery in an adult fly model
messages.body:
Dear Professor Claridge-Chang,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a model using that wiring could learn to make better decisions through experience and feedback.

Your group's work on synthetic memory induction and dopamine's effects on attraction and aversion connects to something I'm trying to figure out: how should I give the model feedback so it learns something useful for unfamiliar positions, rather than just repeating answers it has seen? I also want to understand how to tell a lasting memory apart from an immediate response to stimulation.

In all six simple tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the other option in only three tests. So it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound, and the chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I have no research adviser. I'd like to develop this into a sound study that I could eventually submit to eLife.

Would you be open to occasional mentorship, starting with how to deliver feedback and test whether it leads to lasting learning? I'd appreciate your honest view of the approach. I can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for your time,
Ethan Ramli
High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

messages.name: Yoshinori Aso
messages.subject: Student mentorship inquiry: memory updating in an adult fly model
messages.body:
Dear Dr Aso,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. Chess got me interested in decision-making, and the public adult fly connectome gave me an idea: could a model using that wiring learn to make useful chess decisions from puzzles and feedback?

Your work with Gerald Rubin on how different dopamine neurons write and update memories seems especially useful for a problem I'm stuck on. I need to understand which reinforcement pathways to use and when to give feedback, particularly when a previously rewarded choice is no longer rewarded.

In all six simple tests, the model preferred the rewarded option more after training. But when I changed which option earned the reward, it chose the other option in only three tests. So it failed the full test. I haven't established whether the mechanism is biologically sound, and the chess part currently records feedback without learning from it.

I'm unsure whether the problem is the learning rule, feedback timing or training experience.

I define the research question and training rubric, AI makes most of the code, and I am still learning the underlying methods. I don't have a research adviser and would like to turn this into a sound study, with the hope of eventually submitting it to eLife.

Would you consider occasional mentorship, starting with the learning mechanism and this reversal problem? I'd value an honest assessment of whether the approach makes sense. I can send a one-page methods summary first.

Thank you for considering it,
Ethan Ramli
High-school student | Jakarta, Indonesia

messages.body:
Dear Dr Jefferis,

I'm Ethan Ramli, a 16-year-old Singaporean grade 11 student in Jakarta. I enjoy chess, and discovering the public adult fly connectome made me wonder whether a model using that wiring could learn to make better decisions through experience and feedback.

Your group's work on adult fly circuits and connectomics seems useful for checking a basic assumption in my project.
